newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Child labour a vicious circle in India.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Child labour a vicious circle in India.

text.p: Radha Singh says her energetic 10-year-old son is a problem child.

"He keeps saying he wants to go to school instead of working," explained Singh, a Delhi slum dweller, as the boy dances around her, trying to get her attention. "Things can get really difficult when he fusses."
Her son Ram Lakhan, a scrawny boy with glossy black eyes, works as a mechanic's apprentice at a shop on the dusty outskirts of Delhi.
He is one of tens of millions of Indian children who work instead of going to school, often to support their unemployed parents.
INDIA, HOME TO WORLD'S LARGEST CHILD WORKFORCE
The Labour Ministry says India is home to about 20 million child workers.

But child's rights activists say there are more than 60 million children working in labour-intensive industries such as quarrying, tanning, bangle-making, fireworks factories, match- and brick-making and carpet-weaving.
India officially prohibited the employment of children under 14 years in 1948, and in 1986 barred child labour in 17 industries considered hazardous.

"The fact that children have to work for a living is by itself hazardous to their lives. Why make this distinction?" said Enakshi Ganguly-Thukral, a volunteer at the Coalition Against Child Labour (CACL).

CACL, an umbrella organisation of about 700 Indian social activist groups, says 85 percent of India's child workforce is not officially illegal, and is campaigning for all forms of child labour to be banned.
RURAL POVERTY MAIN CAUSE OF CHILD LABOUR

Most children work on farms and in roadside tea stalls, working to repay their parents' debts to rural loan sharks. CACL says many are pledged as bonded labour to factory owners or their agents in exchange for small loans.

"Children are employed because they constitute cheap labour -- a force that can be bullied into obedience, because they are unable to organise themselves against exploitation in the way that adults can," Ganguly-Thukral said.

"The persistence of child labour depresses wages and contributes to adult unemployment. It perpetuates child labour as children grow up into unskilled, debilitated adults, and then their children must work to support them."
Children working as servants in affluent households are a common sight in Delhi. Most come to the capital with their parents, who migrate from villages in hope of employment.

Many young girls, denied schooling opportunities that boys are given, end up as maids for richer children or as prostitutes. CACL says nearly one-third of the sex workers in six major Indian cities are less than 20 years old.
AVERAGE CHILD GETS PAID $2.50 A MONTH
As unskilled labour, children on average get paid about 90 rupees ($2.50) a month for working 12 hours a day, often in unsafe working conditions with limited access to food and toilets, CACL says.
"Child labour is both a cause and effect of illiteracy and of ignorance and of poor standards of living," said Solomon J.P., another CACL volunteer.
Attending school is optional in India. The government says it plans to introduce a law to make primary education compulsory, which would pull children out of factories and into schools.
While 14 Indian states aim to provide compulsory elementary education, there are currently no federal laws to enforce it.
A senior Labour Ministry official explained: "It was pointed out that if we prosecute parents for not sending their children to school, we will have more parents in jail than children in school."
Solomon said the spread of child labour was nourished by social customs.
"Poor people see other people's children working and so they send their children to work too. Rich people see children working in others' homes, so they employ them too. It's a culture," he said.
Ram Lakhan says he works for 11 hours every day and gets paid 100 rupees a month in return. His parents, who are unemployed, have seven children, six of whom work.
Ram Lakhan attended school until he was seven years old, when he got the job at the motor workshop.
"When I tell the shopowner I want to study, he beats me. I work to eat," he says solemnly.
"But I like studying. When I grow up, I will study and I will teach others. Or maybe, if I can't, I'll open a car repair shop of my own." ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
